title: Meet the Likweli: A New Monkey with Orange Lips and a Roar
summary:
In the dense forests of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), a striking monkey with a crest of spiky hair and a bright orange-cream patch around its mouth has been hiding in plain sight. Called Likweli by locals, it is only the fifth new African monkey species discovered in the past 75 years. Adults weigh about 15 pounds (6.8 kg), roughly the size of a small dog.

The Likweli lives high in the forest canopy in small groups averaging about six individuals. They usually watch human visitors silently from the trees, but their loud, roar-like calls are hard to miss. An explorer first captured the monkey on camera in 2008, but the photo was too blurry to identify. It then disappeared from view until 2018, when local field researcher Jean-Pierre Kapale spotted it during a routine inspection in Lomami National Park in central Congo. His photographs prompted an international team led by John Hart of the Lukuru Wildlife Research Foundation to search for more evidence. Over several years, they recorded 114 observations of the elusive animal.

It was clear the monkey was unique, but the team needed physical evidence to formally confirm it as a new species. They got their chance in April 2021, when park guards seized three Likweli carcasses. The monkeys had been killed for their meat. This allowed scientists to examine the primate closely and collect DNA samples. The monkey's physical features, DNA, and unusual calls all confirmed it was indeed a new species. They named it Colobus congoensis, meaning 'from Congo.' Genetic testing revealed its closest known relative is the black colobus monkey, which lives more than 700 miles (1,100 km) away in west-central Africa. The two species likely split from a common ancestor about 4 to 5 million years ago. The findings were published in the journal PLOS One on July 15, 2026.

Now, researchers are concerned about the Likweli's future. It lives in an area of only about 656 square miles (1,700 sq. km), most of which lies within Lomami National Park. It also faces threats from hunting and habitat loss. Hart and his team have proposed that the Likweli be classified as Endangered. They hope this status will help protect the monkey and its forest home for generations to come.
why_it_matters: This story shows that scientists are still finding large mammals we never knew existed — but it also shows how fragile those discoveries are, because the species was confirmed only after three monkeys had already been killed, and protecting what remains now depends on conservation choices made by governments, parks and local communities.

background_read: The Democratic Republic of the Congo (the DRC — a large country in central Africa whose territory is mostly covered by the Congo Basin rainforest, the second-largest rainforest on Earth after the Amazon) holds some of the least-studied forests in the world.
Lomami National Park, where the Likweli was found, is a protected area in central DRC created in part to guard forests that scientists had barely surveyed.
Colobus monkeys are a group of African monkeys named for their reduced thumbs; the word 'colobus' comes from a Greek word meaning 'mutilated.'

In taxonomy, the science of naming living things, a new species can rarely be confirmed from blurry photographs — researchers normally need a body, a DNA sample or recordings of distinctive calls, which is one reason discoveries like this can take more than a decade.
Scientists describe new mammals every year, but a new primate is a much rarer event, and hunting for bushmeat plus forest clearing are the biggest threats to primates across Africa.

perspectives.description: For researchers, the Likweli is a rare win: a large mammal still unknown to science in a region that has been barely surveyed. They argue that describing and naming a species is the first step toward protecting it, because an unnamed animal with no legal status is easy to lose quietly. The DNA work also fills in the evolutionary tree of Africa's colobus monkeys.

perspectives.perspective: Critics of how the discovery happened
perspectives.description: Some may point out that the science arrived only after three monkeys had already been killed for their meat, so confirmation came at a cost. Others note that local people clearly knew the Likweli long before outsiders did, and that calling it a 'discovery' hides years of local knowledge.

The Likweli fits a pattern: many recently described primates are 'cryptic' species that look like known animals until DNA reveals otherwise, and the Congo Basin is one of the last places where such finds are still likely. At the same time, hunting pressure and forest loss are shrinking primate ranges across Africa faster than new species can be described.

The real test is what an Endangered listing would change on the ground. Supporters hope it brings funding, stronger patrols inside Lomami National Park and international attention; others warn that protection rules can clash with the needs of people living around the park, so any plan will have to be built with local communities.
